b: Taylor Stitch Ojai Corduroy Chore Coat. I’m a big corduroy appreciator. It’s one of my favorite fabrics, and I own a pair of corduroy pants that get a lot of wear. I even have a corduroy suit that I sport during the fall and winter. It’s cozy and taps into my inner 1970s dude. I’ve now added another piece of corduroy to my wardrobe: an everyday jacket. With big patch pockets and a pointed collar, the Ojai is Taylor Stitch’s take on the French chore coat that laborers and farmers wore in the 19th century. It’s cozy and looks good and of course has that unbeatable corduroy texture. It’s not cheap (around $250 at full price), so keep an eye out for a sale this Black Friday.

Oasis. Like a lot of 40-something dudes, I was a big Oasis fan in middle school and high school. Listened to them all the time. Had a poster of them on my wall. They even inspired me to get my first electric guitar, a Peavey Raptor. I learned how to play “Wonderwall” and “Champagne Supernova” on it. I remember getting into a heated debate with my mom in our Toyota Previa when I was in eighth grade, arguing that Oasis would be bigger than the Beatles one day. I don’t think I’ve lost that debate — yet. Ha! So it’s been a pleasant surprise that my kids recently discovered Oasis, and we’ve been listening to (What’s the Story) Morning Glory? quite a bit in the car. I forgot how great of an album it is, and I’ve enjoyed sharing it with my kids and telling them Oasis-related stories from my younger days.

The Complete Tightwad Gazette. My very first blog, which I started in 2005, was called The Frugal Law Student. I shared ways to save money when you’re a broke law student, and a place where I got a lot of ideas for that quest was The Tightwad Gazette. It was a newsletter Amy Dacyczyn published out of Maine from 1990 to 1996, full of advice on how to be frugal and pinch a penny. The issues were later compiled into one big book that runs over 900 pages. I still have a copy, and I still go to it every now and then. A lot of the advice is dated (“Spray WD-40 on your worn typewriter ribbon to squeeze a few more uses out of it.” Don’t think too many people use typewriters these days), but there’s still some solid, timeless advice in there. With stuff getting more and more expensive, we’re all looking for ways to save some money, and this is a good resource. It’s also just fun to step back in time and see how people stretched their budget 30 years ago.

Feelings Without Emotion: Rethinking Male Friendship and the Value of Personal Reticence. Durham University anthropologist Tom Yarrow spent over four years working alongside a group of mostly retired men at a heritage steam railway in northern England. He found they built close friendships while rarely talking about their feelings. They bonded through shared work and a lot of banter — including good-natured teasing. We’ve talked about how making female friendship, with its emphasis on emotional disclosure, the ideal is doing a disservice to men. A lot of guys don’t want to talk about their feelings, and that’s okay. You can just hang out with your bros and still form close and rewarding bonds. You can listen to Yarrow talk about his experience and findings on this Guardian podcast.

The everyday cares and duties, which men call drudgery, are the weights and counterpoises of the clock of time, giving its pendulum a true vibration and its hands a regular motion; and when they cease to hang upon its wheels, the pendulum no longer swings, the hands no longer move, the clock stands still.
